accuracy.evidence: Shape language checked against Development Matters 2021 (3-4 year olds talk about and identify 2D shapes such as circles, rectangles and triangles using informal and mathematical language: sides, corners, straight, flat, round) and the KS1 Year 1 programme of study (recognise and name common 2D shapes, including in different orientations and sizes). Definitions are the true ones: a triangle is closed with 3 straight sides, a square has 4 equal sides, a rectangle has opposite sides equal; the adult text says a square is strictly a special rectangle so nothing taught is false.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented prototype errors from early-geometry research: a square on its vertex called a diamond, only upright equilateral triangles accepted, every quadrilateral called a square, an oval called a circle, and open or curved-sided figures accepted as triangles. Each one appears as a sorting card, a prediction or a challenge option.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagshape has its own mechanisms: tap-to-number each vertex, a triangle versus look-alike sort with open and bendy-sided figures, a square versus rectangle sort with equal-side tick marks, a stick builder that checks side count and short/long mix, and a drawn room to hunt shapes in. flagfit (shape sorter holes and rolling) shares none of these; the 6-token shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds the rules by doing: numbers appear on each tapped corner and the total is said, the gap triangle turns red with 'the 3 sides must join up', four long sticks are refused for a rectangle with '2 long and 2 short', and tapping the egg for a circle says it is an oval. The text after each task only confirms what the child just saw.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions, each with the tempting wrong answer first: '4' corners for a triangle (the child then counts 3 on screen) and 'A diamond, not a square' for a tipped square, which the sort then disproves with equal-side ticks and the message that turning does not change it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged wrong options, each naming the slip: four corners for a triangle, no corners confused with three, a turned square called a triangle or a new diamond shape, 2 long 2 short called a square, an egg called a circle, a window called a circle, and a gapped figure accepted because it has 3 sides or corners.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the family readability limits; kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday objects (plate, door, egg, ruler). Adult text was cut into shorter sentences to pass FK 10 and uses the exact terms 2D shape, side, corner, vertex, right angle, closed shape, orientation, oval and rectangle.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed with no stock phrases. Each kid paragraph is one property with an example; adult paragraphs give the curriculum, the precise definitions, named mistakes and what the lab does. Explanation overlap with every other lesson, including 246 fitting shapes, is under the 12 percent limit.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on iPhone 13 light and 360x640 Android dark for all six steps: the triangle, corner dots and count fit, sort boxes sit side by side under the card, stick piles and the four stick buttons wrap cleanly, and room objects are labelled. Plate and sandwich touched at 360 px so the sandwich and book were moved right and re-checked.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs axe run found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark on desktop and iPhone, and no console errors. Every canvas action has a labelled button (Count the next corner, Put it in Triangle, Add a long stick, Join the sticks into a shape, The plate) and the canvas aria-label reads each result aloud.

sources: DfE (2021) Development Matters: Mathematics, shape and space (3 and 4 year olds; Reception)
DfE (2013) National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study, Year 1 geometry (properties of shapes)
